title: Can the last two digits decide for eight?
description: One hundred and eight and two hundred and eight end in the same two digits, but eight divides only one of them. The video shows why two digits are not enough for eight, and Keeko's doubt about the hundreds digit is broken.
teaching_notes: One idea: a hundred is not a whole number of eights, so the hundreds digit matters, and only a thousand is a whole number of eights, so three digits are needed. Watch for students who carry the rule for four over to eight.

source: Interestingly, even checking for divisibility by 8 can be simplified. Can the last two digits be used for this?
video_script.why: The child compares two numbers that end in the same two digits, finds that eight divides only one of them, and sees that a thousand is the first place value that is a whole number of eights.
video_script.substitution: Find two numbers with the same last two digits and different results, then cut a hundred and a thousand into eights to see which place values leave something over.
video_script.anchor: two number cards, 108 and 208, with their last two digits circled
video_script.wrong_answer: the hundreds digit does not matter for eight
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says the hundreds digit does not matter for eight, because it did not matter for four. One hundred is twelve eights with four left over, and two hundreds leave eight over, which is one more eight, so the bubble is struck through.
video_script.payoff_line: No, the last two digits are not enough for eight

final_answer.value: No: the last two digits are not enough for 8; the last three digits are needed
final_answer.spoken: no, the last two digits are not enough for eight, the last three digits are needed

hold_back: Answer: No: the last two digits are not enough for 8; the last three digits are needed
never_show: the hundreds digit does not matter for 8
maths_rules: 108 and 208 end in the same two digits, 08
104 = 8 x 13 and 112 = 8 x 14, and 108 lies between them, so 8 does not divide 108; 108 = 13 x 8 + 4
the same last two digits give different results, so the last two digits cannot decide for 8
100 = 12 x 8 + 4, so each hundred leaves 4 over; 200 leaves 8 over, which is one more 8, so 200 = 25 x 8
1000 = 125 x 8, so thousands leave nothing over and only the last three digits matter
video_script.design: One idea: a hundred leaves four over when cut into eights, a thousand leaves nothing, so three digits decide. Assumes the test for four on the last two digits. Wrong idea: the hundreds digit does not matter. The two cards stay on the board to the end.
